cards.name: Cold LinkedIn DM / connection message
cards.summary: A connection note plus two or three short follow-up messages that start a real conversation with a stranger on LinkedIn. Good looks like a note that could only have been sent to this one person, a first message that gives before it asks, and an ask small enough to answer from a phone in ten seconds.
use_for: founder-led outbound to a short list of named accounts
SDR or agency social-selling sequences on Sales Navigator
recruiter first touch to a passive candidate
consultant or freelancer reaching a decision-maker after a trigger (new role, funding, a post they wrote)
warming a prospect before a cold email or call
avoid: Pitching in the connection note: the invite gets ignored or declined. Earn the accept with a reason to connect; save the offer for message two or three.
Mass templates with a {first_name} swap and AI flattery ('Loved your inspiring journey'): prospects spot it in one line. Name the one specific thing you saw and why it made you write.
Asking for a 30-minute call in the first message: too big a yes from a stranger. Ask a one-line question or offer a 2-minute asset instead.
Use genre:cold_email when you need length, attachments or a sequence over many weeks; use genre:linkedin_post when the goal is reach, not a 1:1 reply.

sources.title: Upwork: hire LinkedIn Specialists
sources.supports: snippets list LinkedIn outreach / lead generation via Sales Navigator as hired work (page refuses fetchers; snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

buyers: B2B founders and small SaaS teams doing founder-led sales
consultants, CAs, agencies and freelancers selling services
LinkedIn ghostwriting agencies that run the client's inbox
cards.value_why: Upwork runs a LinkedIn Specialists hire category whose listings describe outreach and lead generation via Sales Navigator (snippet-only evidence). Usually sold as a sequence of 3-4 messages plus a personalisation method, often bundled with profile writing.
cards.goal: The prospect accepts the invite and replies to message one with anything other than a no.

structure.does: Gives one specific, true reason you are writing to this person (their post, a shared customer, a trigger like a new role or a city you both sell in). No offer, no link.
structure.length: 1-2 sentences; keep well inside LinkedIn's note limit (check plat: limits; free accounts are tighter)

structure.does: Thanks without gushing, then gives something useful tied to the reason (an observation, a number from their market, a short teardown) and ends with one easy question about their situation.

structure.part: Message 2 (no reply, a few working days later)
structure.does: Adds new value, not a nudge: a relevant example from a similar company, a 2-minute Loom, a one-line insight. Restates the question differently.
Makes it easy to say no or point you to the right person; leaves the door open without guilt.

length.note: Per message. The connection note is the tightest (a character cap, not words); later messages stay short because they are read on a phone in the LinkedIn inbox. Lint counts the whole sequence handed in (note plus up to three messages), so its ceiling is higher than one message.

checklist: Does the connection note name a specific, verifiable reason for writing to this one person?
Is the connection note free of any pitch, price or link?
Does message 1 give something useful before it asks for anything?
Does each message end with exactly one question or one ask?
Is the first ask small (a one-line answer, a yes/no, a 2-minute asset) rather than a 30-minute call?
Would the message still make sense if the prospect's name were removed? (If yes, it is too generic.)
Is every message readable on a phone without scrolling?
Are there zero flattery openers ('inspiring journey', 'came across your profile')?
Does the last message make it easy to say no or redirect?
pitfalls: Opening with 'I came across your profile' or 'Hope you are doing well': it says nothing. Open with the reason: 'Saw your post on PF audit delays at your Nashik plant.'
Writing about yourself for three lines before the reader appears. Flip it: first sentence about them, our product at most one clause.
Personalisation that is only a merge field (company name, city). Use a detail that required reading: a quote from their post, a hiring signal, a product they launched.
Follow-ups that only say 'Just bumping this up'. Each follow-up must carry a new fact, example or asset.
Hinglish or emoji-heavy tone with a senior stranger. Default to plain Indian English; mirror their register only after they reply.
Sending the same sequence to hundreds of people a day: it reads as spam and risks the account. Fewer, researched messages win replies.

ban.label: empty opener
ban.regex: (?i)hope (this|you).{0,20}(finds you|doing) well|i came across your profile

cards.exemplar_brief: LinkedIn connection note plus message 1 and message 2 from the founder of a Pune payroll-compliance SaaS (fictional, 'PayRaksha') to the CHRO of a 400-employee auto-parts maker in Nashik who posted about PF audit headaches. English (Indian). Connection note of 1-2 sentences with no pitch; message 1 under 80 words offering a one-page PF audit checklist; message 2 under 60 words with a new example. Goal: a reply.

verified.note: Note names a real trigger (her PF-audit post, Nashik plant), no pitch or link, about 165 characters. Message 1 (~70 words) gives a usable four-point PF checklist (ECR vs payroll, UAN for contract workers, PF-wage allowances, challan by the 15th) before one easy question; message 2 adds a new example (correctly bracketed, the brief supplied none) and re-asks differently; optional message 3 makes the redirect easy. Small nits: assumes the CHRO is a woman ('after she accepts'); 'fight the same fires' is stock. cards.name: College / scholarship application essay
cards.summary: A first-person essay for undergraduate admission or a scholarship that shows who the applicant is through one specific story and what they made of it. Good looks like a scene only this applicant could have written, a turn in their thinking, and a close that tells the reader how they will show up on campus.
use_for: Common App personal essay and US supplemental essays
UCAS personal statement (2026 entry onwards format)
scholarship essays (foundation, university, corporate CSR)
coaching an applicant from brainstorm to final draft
model essays for an admissions-consulting course or blog
avoid: Writing the essay for the applicant to submit as their own: applicants certify the work is theirs and portals warn about AI use. The PCW job is coaching, structural editing and model essays for fictional applicants.
A resume in paragraphs (Olympiad, JEE rank, MUN, internship): the rest of the application already lists these. Pick one moment and go deep.
A trauma story with no reflection: the reader needs what the applicant did and learned, not only what happened.
For graduate or master's admissions use genre:statement_of_purpose (academic fit, research interest), not this card.

sources.title: Common App: Announcing the 2026-2027 essay prompts
sources.supports: official personal-essay prompts for the 2026-27 cycle

sources.title: UCAS: Writing your personal statement
sources.supports: fetched 2026-10-04: guidance for '2026 entry onwards'; '4,000 characters' overall limit; a section on using AI and ChatGPT and what to avoid so as not to harm the application

sources.title: SOP Expert (India)
sources.supports: Indian agency selling SOP, LOR and admission-essay writing for study abroad

buyers: Class 11-12 students and parents applying abroad (US, UK, Canada, Singapore)
scholarship and CSR foundations that run essay workshops
cards.value_why: Admissions consulting is a paid market; Indian agencies such as SOP Expert sell admission essays alongside SOPs and LORs. The ethical paid work is coaching and editing, priced per essay or per package.
cards.goal: The admissions reader finishes knowing one true, specific thing about the applicant's character that no other part of the file shows, and wants them on campus.

structure.does: Drops the reader into one specific moment (place, object, line of dialogue) that only this applicant lived. No thesis, no quote from a famous person.
Gives just enough background for the moment to matter: what the applicant wanted, what stood in the way.
Shows the change in thinking or action: what they tried, what failed, what they noticed about themselves. This is the heart; reflection in the applicant's own plain words.
One or two later actions that show the change stuck (what they built, taught, changed at home or school).
Returns to an image or line from the opening and points forward to what they will bring to a campus or field; no 'In conclusion'.

length.note: The portal sets the cap: read the Common App prompts page for its personal-essay cap, UCAS (2026 entry onwards) caps the whole statement at 4,000 characters across its questions, and each scholarship sets its own. Write to about 90% of the cap.

checklist: Does the essay open inside a specific moment rather than with a quote, definition or life summary?
Is there one central story rather than a list of achievements?
Could only this applicant have written it (names, places, objects, words their family uses)?
Is there a clear turn: something the applicant thought or did differently by the end?
Does at least half the essay show the applicant acting or reflecting, not describing other people?
Does it sound like a thoughtful 17-year-old, not a thesaurus, a parent or a marketing brochure?
Does the close echo the opening and point forward without 'In conclusion'?
Is it under the portal's cap and does it answer the prompt it is filed under?
Are there zero AI-tell phrases (delve, tapestry, testament to, journey of growth)?
pitfalls: Topic is the activity, not the person ('My internship at a startup'). Fix: the essay is about what the applicant noticed and changed, the activity is the setting.
Grandparent or mentor essay where the applicant disappears. Keep the other person to one paragraph; the rest is the applicant's choices.
Indian-English formalities ('I would like to humbly state', 'since my childhood days') that read as stiff to US/UK readers. Use plain first person and contractions.
Over-polished adult vocabulary that sounds ghostwritten; readers distrust it. Keep the applicant's own phrasing and one or two rough edges.
Moralising last paragraph ('This taught me that hard work always pays off'). Show the lesson through a later action instead.
Copying a famous admitted-student essay's structure beat for beat. Read published examples for range, then build from the applicant's own material.
cards.exemplar_brief: Model Common App personal essay (prompt: a challenge or setback and what you learned) for a fictional 17-year-old from Jamshedpur applying to US engineering programmes; the story is rebuilding the order book of her mother's tailoring shop on WhatsApp after a fire. English (US spelling), 550-620 words, used as a teaching example in an admissions-coaching course, not for submission.

verified.note: 616 words, inside 550-620. Opens inside the fused order-book 'brick', one central story, a real turn (the spreadsheet Ma rejects with 'Who will fill this?'), proof that stuck (cousin's sweet shop), close echoes the brick and the question. Specific to one applicant (Sakchi, Bistupur, Mrs. Hembram's shoulder note), sounds like a thoughtful 17-year-old, no AI tells, no moralising. Only nit: 'junior year' is a US term an Indian Class 11 student would rarely use.

cards.name: Comic / graphic-novel script
cards.summary: A page-by-page, panel-by-panel script that tells the artist exactly what to draw and the letterer exactly what to letter. Good looks like one clear moment per panel, dialogue short enough to fit the art, and reveals timed to page turns (or, for vertical webtoons, to the scroll).
use_for: brand and explainer comics (fintech, health, civic awareness) for Instagram carousels or print
single issues and graphic novels for a publisher or self-published series
vertical-scroll webtoon episodes
4-panel gag strips for social
CSR and government awareness comics in Hindi and regional languages
avoid: Panels that ask for two actions ('He opens the door and then runs down the stairs'): an image freezes one moment. Split it into two panels.
Dialogue that repeats what the art already shows ('Look, it's raining!'). Let the picture carry the fact; dialogue adds attitude or new information.
Prose-novel description (backstory, inner thoughts) in panel notes the artist cannot draw. Describe what is visible; put voice in captions.
For a screen story use genre:screenplay_feature or genre:micro_drama_episode_script; for picture books use genre:childrens_picture_book.
buyers: brands and agencies making branded or explainer comics
NGOs, CSR teams and government departments running awareness campaigns
self-publishing creators and artists who need a writer
cards.value_why: Niche paid market: publishers, webtoon platforms and brand comics. Brand and awareness comics for Instagram are the most frequent paid brief in India; long-form graphic novels pay rarely.
cards.goal: The artist can draw every panel and the letterer can place every word without asking the writer a single question, and the reader turns the page.

structure.does: Title, issue or episode number, total pages, format (print page size, Instagram 4:5 slides, or vertical scroll), and a one-line note on art style and tone.
Starts each page and says how many panels it holds, so the artist can plan the layout. Odd-to-even page turns are where reveals go in print.
structure.length: 1 line per page; usually 3-6 panels per page

structure.does: One frozen moment: shot size (wide, medium, close), setting on first appearance, who is where, the action and the expression that matters. Only what can be drawn.
Numbered under each panel: CAPTION, CHARACTER (dialogue), CHARACTER (whisper/thought/off-panel), SFX. Order = reading order.
structure.length: 0-3 balloons per panel, each a line or two of script

structure.does: Ends the last panel of a right-hand page (or the bottom of a scroll section) on a question, a reveal set-up or a punchline beat.
structure.length: the final panel of the page

length.note: Driven by format: a brand carousel comic is 4-10 pages (one per slide), a gag strip is one row of 3-4 panels, a print issue runs to the publisher's page count. Webtoon episodes are measured in panels and scroll length; agree the count with the platform or client before writing.

checklist: Does every page start with a PAGE heading and a panel count?
Does every panel describe exactly one drawable moment?
Is the setting described the first time it appears and only changes noted after that?
Are all lettering lines numbered, labelled (CAPTION / NAME / SFX) and in reading order?
Does any panel carry more than three balloons? (It should not.)
Does dialogue add something the art does not already show?
Does each page (or scroll section) end on a beat that makes the reader continue?
Is the format stated (print page, 4:5 slide, vertical scroll) so the artist knows the canvas?
For brand or awareness comics, is the key message delivered by a character's action, not a lecture caption?
pitfalls: Talking heads for a whole page. Vary shot size and give characters something to do with their hands.
A brand comic that ends with a caption listing product features. Make the product solve the character's problem on panel; put the CTA in the final slide caption only.
Too many panels on an Instagram slide: text becomes unreadable on a phone. Use fewer, larger panels per slide.
Hindi dialogue written in formal shuddh Hindi for a street-level story. Write the way the characters speak (Hindustani or Hinglish) and keep spelling consistent for the letterer.
Webtoon scripts paced like print pages. In vertical scroll, empty space and panel height control timing; mark long gaps before reveals.
cards.exemplar_brief: Four-page Instagram carousel comic (one page per 4:5 slide, 3-4 panels each) for a fictional Lucknow small-savings app, 'GullakPe': a chai-stall owner learns to set aside Rs 20 a day through UPI round-ups. Script format with PAGE / PANEL headings, panel descriptions in English, dialogue in Hinglish (Roman), final slide caption with the CTA.

verified.note: Full header (format 4:5, 1080x1350, art and tone, cast), PAGE n (x panels) on every page, one drawable moment per panel with shot size, numbered lettering in reading order, never more than three lines a panel. Page ends land (no savings, 'Ek mahina dekh lo', 'Phir se udhaar, Munna?'), the product solves Munna's problem on panel (round-ups on his outgoing milk and kirana payments, Rs 20 x 30 = Rs 600 kettle), CTA only in the last caption. Natural Lucknow Hinglish. Nits: a sweater on a monsoon morning; 'Episode 1 of 1'. CARD FIX: platforms -> add "plat:instagram_carousel" (the exemplar and pitfalls are Instagram slides; the writer had to find the platform card alone). | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): platforms now lists plat:instagram_carousel; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Comment and reply writing (community management)
cards.summary: Replies to comments, reviews and DMs on the brand's own posts, plus value-adding comments on other accounts' posts, written in the brand's voice. Good looks like a reply that answers the exact thing the person said, keeps the thread alive or moves a problem to a private channel fast, and reads well to everyone else scrolling past.
use_for: daily reply coverage on a D2C or creator account
saved-reply libraries for FAQs, complaints and trolls
Google review replies for local businesses
founder or brand comments on creators' and industry posts to borrow reach
first public response while a complaint is resolved in DM
avoid: Arguing with an angry customer in public: every reader judges the brand on tone. Acknowledge, move to DM with a specific route, then post a short public follow-up once solved.
Copy-paste replies ('Thanks for your love!') under every comment: it reads like a bot. Reference the specific word, product or question each person used.
Asking for phone numbers or order IDs in a public reply: personal data in public. Ask them to DM it.
For a formal public statement on an incident use genre:crisis_statement or genre:apology_statement, not a comment.

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: Upwork's list of freelance writing job types; no writing-only community-reply category, so the work is bought inside social media management

buyers: D2C brands and their social agencies
creators and personal brands with busy comment sections
local businesses replying to Google reviews
founders who comment on industry posts to build reach
cards.value_why: Bought as part of social media management retainers (Upwork lists social media managers as a hire category); no writing-only category found. The sellable writing deliverable is a saved-reply library plus voice rules.
cards.goal: The commenter feels heard and either replies again or moves to DM, and anyone reading the thread sees a brand that listens.

structure.does: Mirror the specific thing they said (the product, the word, the problem) so the reply could not sit under any other comment.
Give the actual answer, a useful detail, or a light joke that fits the voice. For complaints: own the experience without blaming the customer.
A question back that keeps the thread going, or a precise route to resolution ('DM us your order number, we'll fix it today').
After the DM fix, a short reply in the original thread saying it was resolved, without private details.

length.note: Per reply. Compliments and emoji comments get one line; questions and complaints need the full acknowledge-answer-next-step shape. Outbound comments on others' posts run 2-4 lines and carry one specific point.

checklist: Does the reply reference something specific from the comment it answers?
Does it answer the actual question asked (price, size, delivery date) rather than redirect by default?
For a complaint, does it acknowledge the problem without blaming the customer and give a precise private route?
Does it avoid asking for phone numbers, addresses or order details in public?
Does it match the commenter's language (Hinglish reply to a Hinglish comment)?
Does it make any product claim the brand could not prove (cures, best, guaranteed)? (It should not.)
Would a reader who sees only this reply understand it without the brand's internal context?
For outbound comments, does it add a point, number or experience rather than praise alone?
pitfalls: 'Please check your DM' with nothing in the DM yet. Send the DM first, then reply publicly.
Sarcasm at trolls that wins the joke and loses the customer watching. Reply once with facts or humour aimed at the situation, never the person; ignore repeat trolls.
Replying in English to a Hindi or Hinglish comment: it reads as distant. Match their language and register.
Generic 'Great post!' comments on creators' posts: zero reach, and they look automated. Add one specific insight or a question the creator will want to answer.
Promising refunds, dates or fixes the support team has not confirmed. Check before you promise in public.
cards.exemplar_brief: Five reply drafts for the Instagram account of a fictional Jaipur block-print kurta brand, 'Chhapa Ghar': (1) angry comment about a 9-day delivery delay, (2) Hinglish sizing question for a 5'2'' buyer, (3) a compliment on a new print, (4) a troll calling the brand overpriced, (5) the founder's outbound comment on a fashion creator's post about slow fashion. Match each commenter's language (Hinglish or English); each reply under 50 words.

verified.note: Five replies, each under 50 words, language matched (two Hinglish). Complaint owns the delay, DMs first, gives a same-day route and a public close-out; sizing reply says choose by bust, not height, with bracketed specs; compliment adds a true craft detail (dabu mud resist); troll reply is gracious and fact-based; outbound comment adds the drying-time insight plus a question. Writer slip: '[44 inch] lamba ... ghutne se thoda neeche' is inconsistent (a 44-inch kurta on a 5'2" buyer falls near the ankle); the fall point should be bracketed with the length.

cards.name: Reaction / commentary video script
cards.summary: A script or beat sheet for a video that reacts to, critiques or explains someone else's clip, trend or news moment. Good looks like a clear take stated up front, short source windows that each set up a piece of the creator's own analysis, and commentary that clearly outweighs the borrowed footage.
use_for: YouTube and Instagram reaction or breakdown videos
news and trend commentary from an explainer creator
AI-tool or product claim 'tested' videos
duet and stitch scripts
brand moment-marketing reactions to a viral clip
avoid: Long stretches of the source with a few 'wow' interjections: YouTube treats repurposed content without significant original commentary as reused content. Keep each source window short and follow it with substantive analysis.
Attacking the person instead of the claim: it invites defamation trouble and reads as cheap. Critique what was said or shown, with evidence.
Use genre:video_essay_script when your argument, not a specific clip, is the spine; use genre:newsjacking_post for a static or text reaction.

sources.title: YouTube Help: YouTube channel monetization policies
sources.supports: fetched 2026-10-04: reused content = repurposing content 'without adding significant original commentary, substantive modifications, or educational or entertainment value'; allowed examples include 'Reaction videos where you comment on the original video' and 'Using clips for a critical review'; not allowed: content copied 'without any substantive modifications'

buyers: YouTube and Instagram creators (news, tech, AI, pop culture, finance)
cards.value_why: Creator-written format with no dedicated marketplace category found on 2026-10-04; usually commissioned inside a creator's scripting retainer.
cards.goal: The viewer stays to the end because the creator's take is the value, and leaves able to repeat that take in one sentence.

structure.does: States the creator's verdict or question in one line before any clip ('This AI app claims one prompt builds a full app. I tested it. It doesn't.').
Names the source (who, where, when) and why it is everywhere now; credits on screen.
Each beat plays a short source window, then the creator adds analysis, a counter-example, a demo or data. Mark each window with a timestamp and duration.
structure.length: 3-6 beats; each clip window a few seconds, commentary longer than the clip

structure.does: Saves the strongest evidence or funniest contradiction for the last beat; re-hooks attention before it.
Restates the take in fresh words, says what the viewer should do with it, and asks one specific comment question.

length.note: Shorts and Reels reactions run 30-90 seconds with 2-3 beats; long-form YouTube breakdowns run 8-15 minutes with chapters. Source footage stays a minority of the runtime at every length. Spoken pace is about 2.5-3 words a second: a 60-second Reel holds roughly 140-160 VO words including clip time.

checklist: Is the creator's take stated in the first 5 seconds, before any source clip plays?
Is the source named and credited?
Is every clip window marked with a timestamp and a short duration?
Is each clip followed by commentary that adds analysis, evidence, a demo or a joke the source does not contain?
Does commentary take more runtime than source footage overall?
Does the critique target claims and actions, not the person's identity?
Is the strongest point saved for the last beat?
Does the ending restate the take and ask one specific comment question?
pitfalls: 'No copyright infringement intended' disclaimers in place of transformation: they do not change how the video is treated. Shorten windows and add more of your own analysis.
Reacting to every second of a long clip. Choose the 3-6 moments that support the take and skip the rest.
A take that is only 'this is crazy'. Write the take as a claim someone could disagree with.
Hinglish VO written as translated English. Write it the way the creator speaks on camera and read it aloud.
Reusing a news clip that later turns out to be fake or AI-made. Verify the source before scripting the take.
cards.exemplar_brief: 60-second Instagram Reel / YouTube Short script for an Indian AI-tools creator page reacting to a viral clip of an AI app claiming one prompt builds a complete shop website. Hinglish voice-over (Roman), 3 clip windows of 2-4 seconds each marked with timestamps, commentary that tests the claim on screen, ending with a verdict and one comment question.

verified.note: Take stated in the first 5 seconds before any clip, source credited on screen, three 3-second clip windows with source timestamps, each followed by a longer test beat, strongest point (customer sees 'Order placed', shop gets no alert) saved for last, verdict restated plus one comment question. Pre-scripted test results are flagged honestly ('if your run differs, change the line'). Hinglish reads as spoken. Writer fault: about 228 VO words in 51 seconds of VO slots, so it runs roughly 80-85 seconds, not 60; trim to about 150. CARD FIX: length.note -> add 'spoken pace about 2.5-3 words a second: a 60-second Reel holds roughly 140-160 VO words including clip time'. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): length.note now gives the spoken pace (2.5-3 words a second, about 140-160 VO words for a 60-second Reel); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Community post (Discord / Circle / Skool / Facebook group)
cards.summary: An announcement, discussion prompt, recurring thread or welcome post inside a member community, written so members reply to each other rather than only react to the host. Good looks like a first line that says what to do, one easy prompt with the host's own example answer, and a ritual members come back to every week.
use_for: weekly ritual threads (wins, asks, intros, show-your-work)
welcome and onboarding posts for new members
announcements for calls, launches and rule changes
discussion prompts that surface members' expertise
pinned rules and how-to-use-this-community posts
avoid: Broadcast-only announcements every day: members tune out. Mix in prompts that ask them to share.
Open questions like 'Any thoughts?' that nobody knows how to answer. Ask a specific question and model the answer.
Course-sales copy inside a paid community: members already bought. Sell the next step only when it serves them.
For one-way channels use genre:telegram_channel_post or genre:whatsapp_channel_post; for email use genre:creator_newsletter.

sources.title: Upwork job post (2026): Skool Community Manager for a coaching community
sources.supports: Example of a paid brief that includes writing announcements and engagement posts for a Skool community

sources.title: Fiverr: Social Media Copywriting category (Platform facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: Platform filter gig counts, a supply signal: Discord 5 gigs vs Instagram 1910, so community copy is rarely sold as a standalone gig

buyers: course creators and coaches running Skool, Circle or Discord communities
cards.value_why: Paid community-management briefs on Upwork include writing announcements and engagement posts for Skool communities (example job, 2026); Fiverr lists only 5 Discord copy gigs (2026-10-04), so it is bought inside community-manager roles rather than as writing gigs.
cards.goal: Members reply in the thread and reply to each other, not only to the host.

structure.does: Says what the post is and what to do, readable in a notification or feed preview ('Wins Friday: drop one client win from this week').
One or two lines of context: the ritual, the event, the reason this matters this week.
One specific question or task, with the host's own example answer so the bar feels low.
Tells members how to answer (a template, a number, a screenshot) so replies are easy to scan and respond to.
Host's first comment, tagging two quiet members, and a recap or spotlight later in the week.

length.note: Ritual threads and prompts stay under about 120 words; welcome posts and rule posts run longer because they are pinned reference.

checklist: Does the first line say what the post is and what members should do?
Is there exactly one prompt or ask?
Does the host model an answer so members know the expected size and tone?
Is the reply format clear enough that a member can answer in under two minutes?
Does the post invite members to respond to each other, not only to the host?
Does it avoid income or result claims the host cannot prove?
Is it scannable on a phone (short lines, no wall of text)?
For recurring rituals, is the name and day consistent with earlier weeks?
pitfalls: Fake engagement bait ('Type YES if you agree!'): cheap replies, no conversation. Ask for something members have and others want (a win, a template, a mistake).
Welcome posts that list rules before warmth. Lead with who is here and what newcomers should do first; link rules after.
Screenshots of members' earnings or results used to sell: needs consent and can be a misleading income claim.
Posting the same ritual at random times. Fix the day and time so it becomes a habit.
Writing like a brand newsletter. A community post is one person talking to a room; first person and names work.
cards.exemplar_brief: Weekly 'Wins Friday' thread for a paid Skool community of about 600 freelance video editors run by a fictional Bengaluru coach who teaches them to land Indian D2C clients. Indian English with light Hinglish; under 150 words; includes the host's own example win and a three-line reply template. Goal: members post one win and one ask, and reply to at least one other member.

verified.note: First line says what and what to do, host models a specific win and a genuine ask (pricing a five-reel pack), three-line template, explicit nudge to answer another member, follow-through comments planned. 122 words, scannable, light Hinglish. Weaker spots: no real 'why now' (the Namaste line is framing, not context); template line 3 'Replying to: [member name]' is confusing inside a member's own top-level reply.

cards.name: Comparison article (X vs Y)
cards.summary: A head-to-head article comparing two products, tools or options on the criteria a buyer actually decides on, ending in who should pick which. Good looks like a verdict in the first screen, firsthand testing with dated numbers, fair wins and losses on both sides, and a 'pick X if / pick Y if' close.
use_for: SaaS and software 'X vs Y' blog posts
personal-finance comparisons (two credit cards, two term plans, two brokers)
consumer tech and appliance head-to-heads
affiliate and review sites
answer-ready pages that AI search can cite for 'X or Y' questions

structure.does: Names both options and the decision ('Zoho Books vs Tally Prime for a 10-person services firm'); one or two lines on who this is for.
Answer first: pick X if..., pick Y if..., in plain sentences an AI answer could quote.
The 6-10 criteria that drive the decision, with values and a dated check note.
What was tested, by whom, on which plan or version, on what date; any relationship with either vendor.

Are prices and features dated with the check date?
Does each option win at least one criterion where that is true?
Is every comparative claim something the writer could prove if challenged?

Does each criterion section end with who wins for which buyer?
Is a third alternative named for readers neither option fits?

Criteria chosen to make the sponsor win. Pick criteria from buyer questions (sales calls, reviews, forums) before you test.
A 300-word intro on 'what is accounting software'. The reader already knows; AI summaries cover it. Start with the verdict.
Foreign prices only for an Indian audience. Give INR prices with GST treatment where the product sells in India.
Never updating. Add a 'last checked' line and refresh when either product changes pricing or plans.

fintech and insurance comparison widgets

Does every row label carry its unit where a number follows?
Is every cell a value or short qualifier rather than an adjective?

cards.name: Condolence message
cards.summary: A short message of sympathy to a bereaved person or family, sent as a card, letter, WhatsApp message or public statement. Good looks like the person who died named and remembered with one specific detail, the reader's grief acknowledged without advice, and, in personal messages, one concrete offer of help.
use_for: personal WhatsApp or card messages to a friend or colleague's family
manager or HR condolence to an employee's family
company statements on the death of a founder, employee or partner
leaders' and public figures' condolence posts (shok sandesh) in Hindi and English
school and institution notices to students and parents
avoid: Explaining or reframing the death ('everything happens for a reason', 'at least he is no longer in pain'): it hurts. Acknowledge the loss and stop.
Making it about yourself ('I know exactly how you feel', a long story of your own loss). One line of shared memory is enough.
'Let me know if you need anything': it puts the work on the grieving person. Offer something specific with a time.
A full life story belongs in genre:obituary or genre:eulogy, not a condolence message.
buyers: leaders' and politicians' offices (official condolence posts)
cards.value_why: No meaningful paid market except official statements written by leaders' offices and corporate communications teams.
cards.goal: The bereaved reader feels the person they lost was seen and valued, and knows the sender is there for them in a specific way.

structure.does: Says you heard and are sorry, naming the person who died and their relationship to the reader ('I was so sorry to hear about your father, Sharma ji').
A real detail: something they said, did or were known for. In official statements: their contribution, stated concretely.
Recognises what the family is carrying without telling them how to feel.

structure.part: Concrete offer (personal) or condolence to family and supporters (official)
structure.does: One specific help with a time ('I'll bring dinner on Thursday', 'take all the leave you need; Ritu will cover your accounts'), or the formal condolence line.
A warm sign-off by register: 'With love', 'ॐ शांति', 'May his soul rest in peace', or a prayer line that suits the family's faith. No reply expected.

length.note: WhatsApp and card messages run 30-90 words; letters and official statements up to about 200. Shorter and specific beats longer and general.

checklist: Is the person who died named (with the honorific the family uses)?
Is there one specific memory, quality or contribution, not only generic praise?
Is it free of explanations of the death and silver linings?
Is the sender's own experience kept to one line or less?
In a personal message, is the offer of help specific and time-bound?
Does the closing line suit the family's faith and language?
Is it free of exclamation marks, hashtags and abbreviations like RIP?
Is it short enough to read in under a minute?
pitfalls: Using a religious closing that does not match the family's faith. If unsure, use a neutral line ('Thinking of you and the family').
Abbreviations and emoji strings ('RIP 😢😢'). Write the words; a single 🙏 is the most a WhatsApp message should carry.
Official posts that read like press releases about the leader ('I was deeply honoured to have known...'). Keep the focus on the person who died and the family.
Getting the name, relationship or cause wrong. Confirm details before sending; never mention the cause unless the family has made it public.
Forwarding a ready-made Hindi shok sandesh image. Write two personal lines instead.

ban.label: silver-lining cliché

cards.exemplar_brief: WhatsApp condolence message in Hindi (Devanagari) from a Patna-based bank branch manager to the son of a colleague, Ramesh Prasad ji, who died after 22 years at the branch. Under 90 words; one specific memory of how he trained new cashiers; a concrete offer (the branch will handle the pension and insurance paperwork, and the manager will visit on Sunday); closing line suited to a Hindu family.

verified.note: 88 words of natural Devanagari Hindi. Names Ramesh Prasad ji, 22 years as the branch's backbone, one specific training memory with his line on counting right rather than fast, acknowledges the family's weight, gives the exact offer from the brief (branch handles pension and insurance papers, visit on Sunday), closes with Om Shanti for a Hindu family. No silver linings, no emoji, son's name correctly left as a placeholder. Sender should confirm the remembered line.

cards.exemplar_brief: Refresh of a fictional 2023 blog post 'How to file ITR-4 as a freelancer' on the site of a Jaipur CA firm (demo name 'Bhandari & Mehra Associates') for the current filing season. The original post (AY 2023-24, published July 2023) had these headings: 1. Who can file ITR-4; 2. Section 44ADA in plain words; 3. Documents you need (Form 26AS, bank statements, invoice list); 4. Step-by-step e-filing on the income-tax portal; 5. Five common mistakes (wrong ITR form, foreign-client receipts left out, AIS not reconciled, TDS mismatch, late filing); 6. Due date and late fee. Figures it used for AY 2023-24, all to be re-checked and replaced with dated sources or bracketed: presumptive income 50% of gross receipts under 44ADA, receipts cap Rs 50 lakh, ITR-4 for resident individuals with income up to Rs 50 lakh, due date 31 July 2023, basic exemption Rs 2.5 lakh (old regime). One author tip to keep: 'keep one income register with invoice date, client, amount and TDS so the AIS can be matched in 10 minutes'. Audit finding: sections 3 and 5 still rank and get cited, the post has slipped from position 4 to 14, and the new-regime default is missing. Deliver the refreshed article (1,400-1,800 words, Indian English) with bracketed placeholders for any figure or due date the writer cannot verify, a visible 'Last updated' line saying what changed, and a 6-10 item change log for the client.

verified.note: Delivers audit note with keep/update/add/cut plan, answer-first intro, a visible 'Last updated' line that says what changed, checked sections, new sections (AIS check, worked example, mistakes, belated return, FAQ), removed/merged notes, links and a 10-item change log; URL kept. Tax facts I can check are right (ITR-4 Rs 50 lakh, 44ADA 50% and Rs 50/75 lakh, 44AD 8%/6% and Rs 2/3 crore, Form 10-IEA, 30-day e-verify, single 15 March instalment, 234F, 234A). Audit findings about the original ('2 broken links', 'author tips kept') are invented because nothing of the original was supplied. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> supply the original 2023 post's outline (its headings, the AY 2023-24 figures it used, one author tip) so the refresh has real material to keep, update and cut. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now supplies the original 2023 post's headings, the AY 2023-24 figures it used, an author tip and the audit finding; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Online course / lesson script
cards.summary: The script for one lesson of a creator or edtech course: a promise, one learning objective, the explanation in small chunks, a worked example, a practice task and a recap that leads into the next lesson. Good looks like a learner who can actually do the promised thing by the end, taught in the creator's own spoken voice.
use_for: self-paced video courses on Graphy-, Teachable- or Skool-style platforms
cohort-course live-session scripts and recorded modules
YouTube-to-paid-course conversions
Hinglish skill courses (freelancing, trading basics, Excel, design, AI tools)
free mini-courses used as lead magnets
avoid: Explaining everything about a topic in one lesson: learners stall. One lesson, one objective, one task.
Theory with no worked example: learners understand but cannot do it. Show the steps on a real case before asking them to try.
Reading slides aloud. Write for the ear; put only key terms and numbers on screen.
Formal corporate training and compliance modules belong to genre:elearning_course_script; one-off live teaching sessions are genre:webinar_script.

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: Upwork lists instructional design among freelance writing job types, with its own typical hourly band (harvest value evidence: $20-$45/hr)

buyers: experts (CAs, designers, traders) turning knowledge into a course
cards.value_why: Upwork lists instructional designers as a writing job type ($20-$45/hr band, 2026-01-21); Fiverr has an e-learning content development subcategory. Often sold per module, together with slide and worksheet copy.
cards.goal: The learner completes the practice task, can do the lesson's one skill, and starts the next lesson.

structure.does: Names the result the learner will have by the end of this lesson and why it matters to them now.
One observable objective ('By the end, you'll write a GBP description that ranks for your area'), linked to the previous lesson.
The idea broken into 2-4 small steps, each with an analogy or picture from the learner's world, checked with a quick question.
The creator does it on a real case, step by step, saying why at each step; screen or on-camera cues marked.
The one error most learners make here and how to spot it.
A specific task doable in about 15 minutes, with what 'done' looks like and where to post or submit it.
Three-point recap and a one-line teaser for the next lesson.

length.note: Driven by the size of the objective. If a lesson runs much past 15-20 minutes it usually holds two objectives; split it.

checklist: Does the lesson state one observable objective near the start?
Does it connect to the previous lesson?
Is the concept split into small chunks, each with an example from the learner's world?
Is there a worked example done step by step on a real case?
Does it name the most common mistake and how to catch it?
Is there a practice task with a clear 'done' standard and a place to submit it?
Does it close with a recap and a reason to start the next lesson?
Is it written for speaking (short sentences, contractions, screen cues marked)?
pitfalls: Long intros about the creator in every lesson. Introduce yourself once in lesson 1.
Jargon defined after it is used. Define it the first time, in plain words, with an example.
Practice tasks like 'Try it yourself' with no deliverable. Say exactly what to produce and how to check it.
Hinglish that switches to formal Hindi in technical parts. Keep English technical terms the learner will see in the tool.
Income or result promises inside lessons ('you will earn 1 lakh in a month'). Teach the skill; leave outcome claims out.
cards.exemplar_brief: Script for Lesson 3 of a paid Hinglish course by a fictional Indore creator who teaches local shop owners to use Google Business Profile: 'Get your first 10 Google reviews this week'. Hinglish (Roman), to-camera with marked screen-recording cues; 8-10 minutes (about 1,100-1,400 spoken words); ends with a practice task (send a review-request WhatsApp to 15 past customers) and a teaser for Lesson 4.

verified.note: Hook (Maps comparison), one observable objective linked to Lesson 2, four chunks each with a desi analogy (wedding card, Maps pin) and a check question, a step-by-step worked example on a labelled demo shop with screen cues, the most common mistake (incentivised reviews, correctly against Google policy), a 15-minute task with a 'done' standard and a place to post it, three-point recap and Lesson 4 teaser. About 1,380 words incl. cues, written for speaking. Nit: switches between aap ('kijiye') and tum ('maango', 'likho') forms; pick one register.

cards.name: Cover letter
cards.summary: A short letter that connects a candidate's strongest proof to one specific job and company and asks for the interview. Good looks like an opening tied to what the company is doing now, one or two quantified accomplishments matched to the job's top requirements, and a clear ask, all in under a page.
use_for: applications where a letter is requested or optional
career switches that the resume alone cannot explain
applications to startups and small firms where a founder reads it
referral and cold applications sent by email
internal moves and promotions
avoid: Repeating the resume line by line: the reader already has it. Pick the one or two proofs that match this job and give the context the resume lacks.
One generic letter for every company: it shows. Name the company's product, market or recent move and why it matters to you.
Opening with 'I am writing to apply for the post of...': the subject line already says that. Open with the connection between your proof and their need.
Use genre:resume for the record of experience and genre:cold_linkedin_dm for a first touch with no open role.

sources.title: Fiverr Writing & Translation: Cover Letters
sources.supports: cover letters are a category on Fiverr's Writing & Translation menu

buyers: job seekers from freshers to senior managers
cards.value_why: Fiverr runs a Cover Letter category; often sold bundled with resume and LinkedIn profile writing.
cards.goal: The hiring manager invites the candidate to interview.

structure.does: Addresses a named person (hiring manager or team lead) where it can be found.
Names the role and connects the candidate's headline proof to something specific the company needs or is doing.
One or two accomplishments that match the job's top requirements, each with context, action and a number.
A specific reason (product, users, market, recent launch) and what the candidate would do in the first months.
Asks for the interview or a short conversation and gives availability; thanks without grovelling.
Name, phone, LinkedIn or portfolio link.

length.note: Under one page. Shorter for startups and email applications; longer only when a career switch needs explaining.

checklist: Is it addressed to a named person where one could be found?
Does the first paragraph link the candidate's proof to a specific company need?
Does it include at least one quantified accomplishment matched to the job description?
Does it say something about the company that could not be said about a competitor?
Is it free of resume repetition and generic traits (hard-working, team player)?
Does it end with a clear ask for an interview or conversation?
Is it under one page and free of typos in names and titles?
Does it read like the candidate speaking, not a template?
pitfalls: 'Kindly find attached my resume' and other old Indian-English letter formulas. Write in plain, direct modern English.
Apologising for gaps or lack of experience. Reframe with what the candidate did and can do.
Mirroring the job description word for word: reads as keyword stuffing. Use its priorities, in your own words, with your evidence.
AI-polished letters full of 'passionate' and 'dynamic'. Cut every adjective a stranger could claim; keep facts.
Writing about what the job will do for the candidate's growth. Lead with what the candidate will do for the team.

ban.label: template opener
ban.regex: (?i)to whom it may concern|i am writing to (apply|express)

cards.exemplar_brief: Cover letter from Soumya Banerjee (demo name), a Kolkata-based content strategist with 5 years in fintech, applying for 'Senior Content Lead, Vernacular' at Kavach Labs (demo name), a Bengaluru insurtech, addressed to the hiring manager Ananya Rao, Head of Content. Company fact to use: Kavach Labs launched 'Bima in 5 Minutes', a Hindi explainer series for first-time term-insurance buyers in Tier 2 and 3 cities, in April 2026. The job description asks for: owning Hindi, Bengali and Marathi content, building a bench of freelance regional writers, and lowering cost per qualified lead. The one quantified proof: she grew a mutual-fund app's Hindi YouTube channel from 18,000 to 212,000 subscribers in 14 months, and built a bench of 6 freelance Hindi scriptwriters along the way. English (Indian); 250-320 words; ask for a 20-minute conversation; sign-off with phone +91 90000 00001 and linkedin.com/in/soumya-demo.

verified.note: Strong opening thesis (insurance is bought on trust, and that trust is built in Hindi), proof with context, method and a number slot, a concrete 90-day plan (ten Hindi buyer questions, five IRDAI-cleared explainers), a clear 20-minute ask with availability, no template phrases. Weaknesses: the one quantified proof and the 'why this company' reason are both placeholders, so it fails the 'could not be said about a competitor' check as written; 'one result is the one I would bring you' is clumsy. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> name the insurtech with one fact about it (product, launch or market) and give the channel result as a number (e.g. subscribers from X to Y in N months), so proof and 'why this company' can be written. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_b): exemplar_brief now names the insurtech with a product fact and gives the channel result as a number (18,000 to 212,000 subscribers in 14 months); re-judge pending.

cards.summary: A creator's own recurring newsletter, often on Substack or beehiiv, free or paid, that turns followers into an audience the creator owns. Good looks like one strong idea per issue in a consistent voice and format, a personal opening, something readers want to forward, and, for paid tiers, a clear promise of what subscribers get.
use_for: weekly or fortnightly issues for creators, coaches and consultants
ghostwritten founder and expert newsletters
free issues that build trust before a paid tier
paid-subscriber-only deep dives
moving Instagram or YouTube followers to an email list
avoid: Turning every issue into a sales email: subscribers stop opening. Give a full idea for free; mention the offer in one line.
A different format every week: readers lose the habit. Fix the sections and the send day.
Publishing the creator's reels as text: the newsletter needs its own depth or angle.
A company's brand or product newsletter is genre:editorial_newsletter or genre:product_update_newsletter; link roundups are genre:curated_newsletter.

structure.does: A short first-person moment from the creator's week that leads into the idea.
One idea developed fully: essay, breakdown, how-to, story or teardown, with the creator's own examples and numbers.
The fixed section readers expect (one tool, one reader question, one thing I'm reading).
A one-line takeaway and a specific question readers can answer by hitting reply.
One line on the creator's offer, or what paid subscribers got this week; sponsor slot clearly labelled.

Does it open with a personal, specific moment rather than a greeting?
Does the main piece include the creator's own examples, numbers or experience?
Is the recurring segment in the same place and format as previous issues?
Is there a specific reply question?
Is any sponsored mention clearly labelled?
Is promotion limited to a short, clearly separated mention?
Does it sound like the creator speaking, consistent with earlier issues?
pitfalls: 'Hope you're having a great week!' openers. Start with the moment or the idea.
Teasing the paid tier so hard the free issue feels empty. Free issues build the trust that paid tiers convert.
Ghostwritten issues that lose the creator's phrases and opinions. Interview the creator weekly and keep a voice sheet.
Undisclosed affiliate links or brand deals in a creator's newsletter. Label them where they appear.
Writing for the algorithm (keywords, hashtags) instead of the inbox. Write to one subscriber.
cards.exemplar_brief: Weekly free issue of 'Paisa Patterns', the beehiiv newsletter of a fictional Mumbai personal-finance creator (35k Instagram followers, 6k subscribers): one essay on why her own SIP stopped at month 7 and the two changes that restarted it. Indian English with light Hinglish; 500-700 words; subject line and preview text; a reply question; one line on what paid members got this week. No specific fund recommendations.

verified.note: Subject and preview promise one idea, opens on a specific moment (seven green ticks, then a blank), own numbers and story (debit date on the 5th vs bills on the 1st-7th, Rs 500 floor), two changes clearly argued, recurring 'One-minute check' slot, specific reply question, one paid-members line, no fund names, disclaimer. Light Hinglish lands ('SIP chal rahi hai na?'). Nits: almost no contractions makes the creator's voice a little stiff; 'a couple of missed instalments' undercounts the usual three-failure cancellation, though it is hedged.

cards.name: Crisis / holding statement
cards.summary: The first public statement in a crisis: it acknowledges what happened, states only confirmed facts, puts affected people first, says what is being done and when the next update will come. Good looks like a statement issued fast, in plain words, that nobody will have to retract later.
use_for: first response to an incident (outage, data breach, accident, product contamination, viral complaint)
pre-approved holding statements in a crisis plan
statements for X, LinkedIn, the website, app banners and media queries
employee and partner versions of the same message
follow-up updates as facts are confirmed
avoid: Guessing causes or numbers before they are confirmed: corrections destroy trust. Say what is known and when you will say more.
'We regret any inconvenience' for harm to people: it minimises. Name the harm and what you are doing about it.
'No comment' or silence while the story spreads. A holding statement can be issued before all facts are in.
A full, considered apology after the facts are known is genre:apology_statement; a routine announcement is genre:press_release.

sources.title: Upwork: hire Public Relations Specialists
sources.supports: listing snippets name holding statements, response plans, talking points and spokesperson guidance as crisis work (snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

sources.title: Upwork: hire Corporate Communications Experts
sources.supports: dedicated hire category; snippets list crisis, internal and external communications (snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

buyers: startups after outages, breaches or viral complaints
cards.value_why: Upwork PR specialists list holding statements, response plans and talking points as crisis work; usually bought as part of a crisis-communications retainer or plan, and always reviewed by legal.
cards.goal: Stakeholders know the organisation is aware, is acting, and where and when the next update will come, and nothing in the statement has to be withdrawn later.

structure.does: States the incident in plain words, as confirmed so far, with time and place.
Addresses those affected: their safety, care being provided, and an apology where legal has cleared it.
Only what is verified: scope, who is affected, what is not affected. No speculation on cause or blame.
Concrete steps already under way (suspended, contained, investigating with named authorities, helpline opened).
Specific instructions for affected people (change password, call this number, keep the receipt), with contact details.
When and where the next update will be published.
Spokesperson name and title, date and time stamp.

length.note: Short because speed beats polish. Social versions are cut to the first three parts plus a link; the website and media versions carry all parts.

checklist: Does it say what happened in the first two sentences?
Are affected people addressed before the organisation's reputation?
Is every fact stated confirmed, with nothing speculative about cause or blame?
Are the actions concrete and already under way?
Does it tell affected people exactly what to do and how to reach the organisation?
Does it commit to a time and place for the next update?
Is it free of minimising phrases ('any inconvenience', 'isolated incident') and of 'no comment'?
Is a named spokesperson and a date-time stamp included?
Has legal reviewed it (noted in the hand-off)?
pitfalls: Blaming a named vendor, employee or customer in the first statement. Defamation risk, and the facts may change. Say 'we are investigating with our partner'.
Passive voice that hides responsibility ('mistakes were made'). Say who is doing what.
Different numbers on X, the website and in media quotes. Issue one master text and cut versions from it.
Promising outcomes not yet decided (full refunds, firing staff). Promise only what has been approved.
English-only statements when those affected speak Hindi or a regional language. Issue the language versions together.
cards.exemplar_brief: Holding statement from a fictional Hyderabad food-delivery startup, 'ThaliGo', three hours after reports that about 40 customers in Gachibowli fell ill after orders from one partner kitchen. English; 150-220 words; for X, the website and an app banner. Legal has cleared: kitchen suspended from the platform, affected customers' medical costs covered, Telangana food-safety officials contacted, helpline number to be quoted as [helpline]; next update by 8 pm IST.

verified.note: 208-word master with what happened in the first two sentences, people first, only confirmed facts, every legal-cleared action and nothing more (no apology because none was cleared, flagged in the hand-off), clear instructions with the helpline, 8 pm IST next update, spokesperson and time stamp slots. Cut-downs for X (counted under 280) and an app banner from the same text; hand-off notes cover reported vs confirmed numbers, no kitchen name or blame, Telugu and Hindi versions. No minimising phrases. Signable as is.

cards.name: Review / criticism (film, book, food, tech, culture)
cards.summary: A critic's evaluation of a work or experience that describes it, judges it against a clear standard with specific evidence, and gives the reader a verdict. Good looks like an opening that makes the reader want to read on, claims backed by named scenes, lines, dishes or moments, a fair weighing of strengths and weaknesses, and a 'for whom' verdict.
use_for: film, OTT series and theatre reviews
book reviews for publications, newsletters and creators
restaurant and food reviews
music, gaming and culture criticism
review scripts for YouTube and podcast critics
avoid: Plot summary with a star rating tacked on: that is a recap, not criticism. Describe only enough to support the judgment.
Adjectives without evidence ('brilliant', 'disappointing'): the reader cannot weigh them. Point to the scene, line, dish or page.
Spoilers without warning, and breaking an embargo. Keep it spoiler-free unless clearly marked, and respect embargo dates.
Reviews of buyable products against specs are genre:product_review_article (Google's review guidance applies).

sources.title: Fiverr: Articles & Blog Posts category (Article type facet read 2026-10-04)
sources.supports: Fiverr's 'Review' article type had 679 gigs on 2026-10-04, covering product and culture reviews (a supply signal)

cards.value_why: Fiverr's 'Review' article type (679 gigs on 2026-10-04) covers both product and culture reviews; staff critic roles are shrinking, so freelance demand is mostly creator-led.
cards.goal: The reader knows whether this work is for them and why, and sees it more sharply than before.

structure.does: A vivid entry point (a moment, a line, a taste) that also signals the critic's overall view.
Title, maker (director, author, chef), where and when to find it, runtime or price.

structure.part: What it is trying to do
structure.does: Genre, ambition and context (earlier work, the source, the trend it belongs to), so the standard of judgment is fair.
2-4 claims about what works and what does not, each backed by a specific scene, line paraphrase, dish, design choice or page.
The best case against the critic's view, or the audience who will feel differently.
Who should watch, read or eat this and who should skip it; rating if the outlet uses one.

length.note: Set by the outlet: capsule reviews run 100-300 words, newspaper reviews 500-800, long-form criticism longer. Video scripts follow the same parts in spoken form.

checklist: Does the opening signal the critic's view, not just set the scene?
Are the essentials (title, maker, where, runtime or price) present?
Is plot or description kept to what the judgment needs?
Is every judgment backed by a specific moment, line, dish or detail?
Is the standard fair to what the work is trying to be?
Is there a counterweight acknowledging a different reasonable view?
Does the verdict say who it is for and who should skip it?
Is it spoiler-free, or are spoilers clearly flagged?
Are free screeners, review copies or hosted meals disclosed?
pitfalls: Quoting long passages or lyrics. Paraphrase; quote a short line at most.
Attacking the maker's person rather than the work, or making factual allegations about a restaurant's hygiene you cannot prove. Critique the work and the experience you had.
Reviewing the film you wanted instead of the one made. State the standard, then judge against it.
Cliché praise ('rollercoaster of emotions', 'must-watch'). Name the specific emotion and the moment that caused it.
Writing for fellow critics. Write for a reader deciding how to spend an evening and Rs 500.

ban.label: review cliché
ban.regex: (?i)rollercoaster of emotions|must[- ]watch|edge of (your|my) seat|tour de force

cards.exemplar_brief: Spoiler-free review of a fictional new 8-episode Hindi OTT thriller, 'Sonepur Junction', set around a Bihar railway town, for a Delhi culture newsletter. English (Indian); 600-800 words; claims backed by specific (invented, in-world) scenes; a counterweight paragraph; a 'watch it if / skip it if' verdict; discloses the free screener.

verified.note: Lede (the train a minute early) signals the view; essentials up top; fair standard set (mood-first thriller); claims backed by in-world scenes (PA announcements vs the ghazal radio, the pressure-cooker interrogation, the journalist who explains the plot); a genuine counterweight; watch-if / skip-if verdict and a where-to-start tip; spoiler-free; screener disclosed. Specific, witty without cliche, right register for a culture newsletter.

cards.name: Crowdfunding campaign page
cards.summary: The campaign page and its updates that turn visitors into backers or donors on reward or donation platforms (Kickstarter, Indiegogo, Ketto, Milaap and similar). Good looks like a clear one-line promise, a human story, an exact breakdown of what the money does, honest risks and timeline, and rewards or impact levels that make the next step obvious.
use_for: reward-based campaigns for products, books, comics, games and films
donation campaigns for causes, NGOs and community projects
medical and emergency fundraisers (with care)
campaign video scripts and update posts
pre-launch pages that collect early-bird sign-ups
avoid: Vague asks ('help us make our dream come true'): backers fund specifics. Say what is being made or done, by whom, by when, and what each amount buys.
Hiding risks: missed timelines are common and silence makes them worse. Name the risks and how you will handle them.
Fake countdowns, invented backer numbers or 'only 2 left' when untrue: dark patterns and misleading claims. Use real deadlines and real counts.
Ongoing donor appeals for an established nonprofit are genre:fundraising_appeal; a normal product launch is genre:launch_sequence.

sources.supports: own subcategory; campaign copywriting is a listed option (snippet-only, 2026-10-04)

buyers: authors, comic creators, game developers and filmmakers
NGOs, social enterprises and community groups
families raising medical funds (usually helped by the platform or volunteers)
cards.value_why: Fiverr has a Crowdfunding > Campaign Creation subcategory where copywriting is a listed option; the work is project-based and bundled with video and marketing.
cards.goal: The visitor backs or donates now and shares the campaign with at least one person.

structure.does: What it is and who it is for, in plain words a stranger understands.
Maker on camera: the problem or dream, the thing being made, proof it is real, the ask.
Why this, why these people, why now; one specific person or moment.
Goal amount broken into named uses (printing, tooling, shipping, platform fees, taxes) or impact per amount for donations.
Each tier: what the backer gets, when, and shipping limits; donation levels tied to concrete outcomes.
Prototype photos, samples, past delivery, partners, and who is responsible.
Milestones by month and the real risks with mitigation.
Shipping, refunds, taxes, what happens if the goal is missed; final ask to back and share.

length.note: Reward campaigns with many tiers run longer; urgent medical fundraisers run shorter and lead with the patient's need, treatment and verified costs.

checklist: Can a stranger say what is being funded after reading the title and one-liner?
Is the goal amount broken down into named uses?
Does each reward tier say what, when and where it ships?
Is there real proof (prototype, sample, past delivery, partner)?
Are risks and the timeline stated honestly?
Are all deadlines, counts and scarcity claims true?
Does the page say what happens if the goal is not met?
Does it end with a clear ask to back and to share?
pitfalls: Rewards priced below cost once shipping and taxes are added. Check the numbers with the maker before writing the tiers.
Medical fundraisers that share a patient's private details or photos without consent. Share only what the family approves; keep dignity.
Story about the founders' feelings with no product until paragraph five. Show the thing early.
Updates that only ask for more money. Updates report progress, show the work and thank backers by name or count.
Promising delivery dates the factory or printer has not confirmed. Pad the timeline and explain it.

require.label: says where the money goes or what could go wrong

cards.exemplar_brief: Reward-based crowdfunding page for a fictional Ahmedabad studio funding the first print run of a 200-page Gujarati-English bilingual children's comic of monsoon folk tales; goal Rs 12 lakh. English (Indian); 900-1,200 words; includes a 90-second video script, a 'where your money goes' breakdown, 5 reward tiers with delivery months, risks and timeline, and an ask to back and share.

verified.note: All parts present: clear title and one-liner, a 90-second video script with the ask, a story with one moment, a money breakdown that adds up to Rs 12 lakh, five tiers with what, when and where, proof with placeholders, month-by-month timeline with honest risks and mitigations, FAQ including goal-missed, ask to back and share. Gujarati touches are right (Varsaad ni vaato, Chomasu). Writer fault: the budget lines and 'Rs 5 lakh per the printer's written quote' are invented figures presented as a supplier's quote; mark them illustrative or bracket them. Close is a little stock.

cards.name: Curated link newsletter
cards.summary: A recurring email that selects the day's or week's best links in a niche and adds a short take on why each one matters to this reader. Good looks like a lead item with a real point of view, quick hits that each say 'what happened, why it matters to you', original summaries that link the source, and a format readers can finish in a few minutes.

media-brand and creator daily or weekly briefs
investor and founder newsletters
internal news digests for leadership
community roundups (best posts, jobs, events)
avoid: Pasting headlines with no take: readers can get links anywhere. The take is the product.
Copying paragraphs from the source articles: summarise in your own words and link the original.
Too many links: readers skim past all of them. Cut to the items your reader would act on.

A tool, chart, template or number the reader can use this week.

length.note: Daily briefs stay near the low end; weekly digests carry more items. Every item should earn its place; long issues risk Gmail clipping.

checklist: Does every item include a take on why it matters to this reader, not just a headline?
Is every summary in the writer's own words, with a link to the original?
Is link text descriptive (no 'click here')?
Does the subject line lead with the biggest takeaway?
Is the lead item clearly more developed than the quick hits?
Is sponsored content labelled and separated?
Are facts checked against the original source, not a re-post?
Can the issue be read in about five minutes?
pitfalls: Linking to aggregators or re-posts instead of the original report. Find and credit the primary source.
Takes that only restate the headline ('Big news for D2C!'). Say what changes for the reader: cost, risk, opportunity.
Including an item because it is popular, not because it matters to this audience. Use the 'so what for my reader' test.
Forgetting dates on fast-moving news. Say when something happened or was announced.
Mixing affiliate links into editorial picks without saying so. Disclose them.

cards.name: Brand store / D2C shop copy
cards.summary: Copy for an Amazon Brand Store, Shopify storefront or Instagram shop: the brand hero line, a short brand intro, collection names and intros, product tile lines and a trust strip. Good looks like collections named the way shoppers think (by need or occasion), every claim one the brand can document, and words short enough to read on a phone between images.
use_for: Amazon Brand Store pages
Shopify and other D2C storefront home and collection pages
Instagram and Facebook shop collections
marketplace brand pages (Flipkart, Myntra and similar)
seasonal and sale store refreshes
avoid: Collections named after internal SKU codes or ranges ('Series X Pro'): shoppers cannot find what they need. Name by need, occasion or concern ('For dry skin', 'Diwali gifting under Rs 999').
Superlatives and purity claims the brand cannot prove ('India's No. 1', '100% chemical-free'): misleading-ad rules apply. Use documented facts: certifications, ingredients, review counts.
Long brand essays on a store page: shoppers came to browse. Keep the story to a few lines and link to genre:about_page.
Single-product pages are genre:product_description; Amazon detail-page modules are genre:amazon_a_plus_content.

cards.goal: A shopper landing on the store understands what the brand stands for, finds the right collection in one or two taps, and adds a product to cart.

structure.does: Who the brand is for and its one promise, in shopper words.
Origin, what is different, one proof (certification, sourcing, review count).
Navigation labels by need, concern, occasion or price band.
Who the collection is for and how to choose within it.
One benefit line under the product name, not a repeat of it.
Returns, delivery, payment options, certifications and ratings, only those that are true and current.
Ingredients, craft or sourcing shown with specifics.

length.note: Grows with the number of collections and pages. Store pages are image-led; text is short labels and lines, not paragraphs.

checklist: Does the hero line say who the brand is for and what it promises?
Are collections named by shopper need, occasion, concern or price band?
Does every collection intro help the shopper choose?
Is every claim (natural, certified, bestselling, rated) backed by documentation the brand holds?
Are trust-strip items true today (return window, delivery promise, payment options)?
Do product tile lines add a benefit rather than repeat the product name?
Is terminology consistent with the product listings (same names, same sizes)?
Is the copy short enough to read on a phone between images?
pitfalls: Copying the homepage copy word for word to the Amazon store. Write for shoppers already on Amazon, who compare fast and trust ratings.
Trust strips listing 'Free shipping' when it applies only above a cart value. State the condition.
Sale banners with fake 'ends tonight' timers that reset. Use real end dates.
Hinglish wordplay in navigation labels. Keep labels plain; save wit for hero lines and intros.
Different product names on the store and the listings. Shoppers and AI shopping agents lose the match; use one naming scheme.

Documented proof: 4.3 stars from 1,860 Amazon ratings, as shown on the listings on 1 October 2026. Collections by skin concern, two products each: Dry skin: Rich Coconut Cream 50 g (hero ingredient: virgin coconut oil) and Coconut Body Butter 200 g (shea butter). Dull skin: Turmeric Face Scrub 75 g (turmeric) and Coconut Milk Face Wash 100 ml (coconut milk).
